html:
The East-West Schism is the break between the Latin church of Rome and the Greek church of Constantinople, dated by custom to 1054. It divided Christianity into what became the Catholic Church and the Eastern Orthodox Church, and the split has never healed.

In 1054 papal envoys led by Cardinal Humbert laid a bull excommunicating Patriarch Michael Keroularios on the altar of Hagia Sophia, and the patriarch excommunicated them in turn. At the time it looked like one more quarrel. The deeper differences had grown for centuries:

  • the pope's claim to rule the whole church
  • the Filioque, a Western addition to the creed
  • the use of unleavened bread at Mass
  • married priests and other customs, argued over since the Quinisext Council and the Photian schism

What made the split final was later violence, above all the sack of Constantinople in 1204. Attempts at reunion, such as the Council of Florence in 1439, failed. In 1965 the pope and the patriarch lifted the excommunications of 1054.
